October 28, 2026 
 
Directions under Section 35A read with Section 56 of the Banking Regulation Act, 
1949 – Lokapavani Mahila Sahakari Bank Niyamitha, Mandya - Extension of 
Period 
     The Reserve Bank of India issued Directions under Section 35A read with Section 56 
of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949 to Lokapavani Mahila Sahakari Bank Niyamitha, 
Mandya vide Directive No. BLR.DOS.SSMS.No.S628/09-01-242/2025-2026 dated July 
29, 2025, for a period of six months up to close of business on January 30, 2026.              
The Reserve Bank of India is satisfied that in the public interest, it is necessary to further 
extend the period of operation of the Directive beyond close of business on October 30, 
2026. 
 
2. Accordingly, the Reserve Bank of India, in the exercise of powers vested in it under 
sub-section (1) of Section 35A read with Section 56 of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949, 
hereby extends the Directive for a further period of three months from close of business 
on October 30, 2026 to close of business on January 30, 2027, subject to review. 
 
3. The aforesaid extension and /or modification by the Reserve Bank of India should not 
per-se be construed to imply that the Reserve Bank of India is satisfied with the financial 
position of the bank. 
 
4. Other terms and conditions of the Directive under reference, shall remain unchanged. 
 
 
 
                        (Brij Raj)

October 27, 2026 
 
Reserve Bank holds 36th Conference of State Finance Secretaries 
 
     The 36th Conference of State Finance Secretaries was held on October 27, 2026 
at RBI, Mumbai. The theme of the Conference was ‘Role of Quality of Expenditure, 
Effective Cash and Prudent Debt Management in Enhancing States’ Fiscal 
Sustainability’. The Conference was attended by the Finance Secretaries of 27 States 
and three Union Territories as well as senior officials from the Ministry of Finance, 
Government of India, Controller General of Accounts and the Comptroller and Auditor 
General of India.  Governor, Reserve Bank of India inaugurated the Conference. 
 
     Addressing the participants, the Governor emphasised the importance of 
maintaining the quality of expenditure to ensure the long-term fiscal health of the 
States. He also emphasised on the need for the States to adopt prudent borrowing 
strategies and efficient cash management practices. The Governor urged the States 
to onboard onto the Unified Lending Interface (ULI) and utilise Programmable Central 
Bank Digital Currency (P-CBDC) for Direct Benefit Transfers (DBT). He also advised 
States to make effective use of the State Level Bankers’ Committee (SLBC) forum. 
During the Conference, the Governor released a Booklet titled ‘Compendium on Cash 
and Debt Management for State Governments’. The Booklet summarises relevant 
concepts, operational processes and good cash and debt management practices in a 
concise and accessible format. 
 
     The meeting reviewed, inter alia, market borrowings by the States, short-term 
financial accommodation to the States from Reserve Bank, adoption of Benchmark 
Issuance Strategy by the States, etc. 
 
 
 
                                                                                                           (Brij Raj)

Premature redemption under Sovereign Gold Bond (SGB) Scheme - 
Redemption Price for premature redemption of SGB 2020-21 Series I due on 
October 28, 2026 
 
     In terms of GOI notification F.No. 4(4)-B(W&M)/2020 dated April 13, 2020 (SGB 
2020-21 Series I - Issue date April 28, 2020) on Sovereign Gold Bond Scheme, 
premature redemption of Gold Bond may be permitted after fifth year from the date of 
issue of such Gold Bond on the date on which interest is payable. Accordingly, the 
next due date of premature redemption of the above tranche shall be on October 28, 
2026. 
 
2. Further, the redemption price of SGB shall be based on simple average of closing 
price of gold of 999 purity of previous three business days from the date of redemption, 
as published by the India Bullion and Jewellers Association Ltd (IBJA). Accordingly, 
the redemption price for premature redemption due on October 28, 2026, shall be 
₹14,159/- (Rupees Fourteen Thousand One Hundred and Fifty-Nine Only) per unit 
of SGB based on the simple average of closing price of gold for the three business 
days i.e., October 23, October 26, and October 27, 2026.

ANNEX 
Type of Auction 
1. For multiple price-based auction, successful bids will get accepted at the respective quoted 
yield/price for the security. For uniform price-based auction, bids will get accepted at the cut 
off yield/price accepted in the auction.  
2. The auction will be yield based for new security and price based for securities which are 
re-issued.  
3. In case of a Floating Rate Bonds (FRB), the auction will be spread-based for new security 
and price based for securities which are reissued. At the time of placing bids for new FRB, 
the spread should be quoted in percentage terms.  
Minimum Bid Size 
4. The securities will be issued for a minimum amount of ₹10,000/- (nominal) and in multiples 
of ₹10,000/- thereafter.   
Non-Competitive Segment 
5. In all the auctions, Government security up to 5% of the notified amount for sale of individual 
security will be allotted to the eligible individuals and institutions under the Scheme for Non-
competitive Bidding Facility in the Auctions of Government Securities. Individual investors 
can also place bids as per the non-competitive scheme through the Retail Direct portal 
(https://rbiretaildirect.org.in). 
6. Each bank or Primary Dealer (PD) on the basis of firm orders received from their constituents 
will submit a single consolidated non-competitive bid for individual security on behalf of its 
constituents in electronic format on the Reserve Bank of India Core Banking Solution (e-
Kuber system).  
7. Allotment under the non-competitive segment will be at the weighted average rate of 
yield/price of the successful bids that will emerge in the auction on the basis of the 
competitive bidding. 
Submission of Bids 
8. Both competitive and non-competitive bids for the auction should be submitted in electronic 
format on the Reserve Bank of India Core Banking Solution (e-Kuber system).  
9. Bids in physical form will not be accepted except in extraordinary circumstances.  
Business Continuity Plan (BCP)-IT failure 
10. Only in the event of system failure, physical bids will be accepted. Such physical bids should 
be submitted to the Public Debt Office, Mumbai through (email; Phone no: 022-22603456, 
022-22603457, 022-22603190) in the prescribed form which can be obtained from RBI 
website (https://www.rbi.org.in/Scripts/BS_ViewForms.aspx) before the auction timing ends.  
11. In case of technical difficulties, Core Banking Operations Team should be contacted (email; 
Phone no: 022-69870466, 022-69870415).  
12. For other auction related difficulties, IDMD auction team can be contacted (email; Phone no: 
022-22702431, 022-22705125). 
 
 
Multiple Bids 
13. An investor can submit more than one competitive bid in electronic format on the Reserve 
Bank of India Core Banking Solution (e-Kuber system).  
14. The aggregate amount of bids submitted by an investor in an auction should not exceed the 
notified amount of auction.   
Decision Making Process 
15. On the basis of bids received, the Reserve Bank will determine the minimum price/maximum 
yield up to which tenders for purchase of Government Security will be accepted at the 
auctions.  
16. Bids quoted at rates lower than the minimum price/higher than the maximum yield 
determined by the Reserve Bank of India will be rejected.  
17. Reserve Bank of India will have the full discretion to accept or reject any or all bids either 
wholly or partially without assigning any reason. 
Issue of Securities  
18. Issue of securities to the successful bidders will be by credit to Subsidiary General Ledger 
Account (SGL) or to Constituents’ Subsidiary General Ledger Account (CSGL), maintained 
with Reserve Bank of India. 
Periodicity of Interest Payment 
19. Interest on the Government Security will generally be paid half-yearly other than in case of 
securities with non-standard maturities. The exact periodicity of coupon payment is 
invariably mentioned in the specific notification for the issue of security. 
Underwriting of the Government Securities   
20. The underwriting of the Government Securities under auctions by the ‘Primary Dealers’ will 
be as per the “Revised Scheme of Underwriting Commitment and Liquidity Support” 
announced by the Reserve Bank vide circular RBI/2007-08/186 dated November 14, 2007 
as amended from time to time. 
Eligibility for Repurchase Transactions (Repo)  
21. The securities will be eligible for Repurchase Transactions (Repo) as per the conditions 
mentioned in Master Direction – Reserve Bank of India (Repurchase Transactions (Repo)) 
Directions, 2025 as amended from time to time.  
Eligibility for ‘When Issued’ Trading 
22. The securities will be eligible for “When Issued” trading in accordance with the guidelines on 
‘When Issued transactions in Central Government Securities’ issued by the Reserve Bank 
of India vide circular No. RBI/2018-19/25 dated July 24, 2018 as amended from time to time. 
Investment by Non-Residents 
23. Investments by Non-Residents are subject to the guidelines on ‘Fully Accessible Route’ for 
Investment by Non-residents in Government Securities and other related guidelines as 
issued by the Reserve Bank from time to time.

October 25, 2026 
 
 
Hon’ble Prime Minister of India inaugurates the Reserve Bank of India’s Data 
Centre and Cybersecurity Training Institute in Bhubaneswar, Odisha 
                                                                                                                                                        
     The Hon’ble Prime Minister of India, Shri Narendra Modi, today inaugurated the 
Reserve Bank of India’s newly established Data Centre and Cybersecurity Training 
Institute in Bhubaneswar, Odisha. This marks a significant milestone in strengthening the 
technological foundation of India’s financial system. Hon’ble Governor of Odisha, Shri 
Brajmohan Ram, Hon’ble Chief Minister of Odisha, Shri Mohan Charan Majhi; Hon’ble 
Union Finance and Corporate Affairs Minister, Smt. Nirmala Sitharaman; Hon’ble Union 
Minister for Tribal Affairs, Shri Jual Oram; Hon’ble Deputy Chief Ministers of Odisha, Shri 
Kanak Vardhan Singh Deo and Smt. Pravati Parida, and Hon’ble Members of Parliament, 
Shri Manmohan Samal and Smt. Aparajita Sarangi, also graced the event. 
 
2. In his address, the Hon’ble Prime Minister highlighted the significance of the institutions 
inaugurated today - the Data Centre and the Cybersecurity Training Institute - in 
strengthening India’s digital financial infrastructure and advancing its technological self-
reliance. The PM described the facility as a reflection of India’s changing approach to 
governance focused on taking the benefits of economic development to every region and 
every citizen. He emphasised that a secure banking system needs secure digital 
infrastructure supported by robust data centres and powerful computing systems and 
RBI’s new Data Centre is a critical step in this direction.  
 
3. In her address, the Hon’ble Union Minister of Finance and Corporate Affairs 
underscored the strategic importance of resilient infrastructure in safeguarding financial 
stability and supporting sustained economic growth. She further said that the new Data 
Centre will house RBI’s mission-critical systems, including RTGS and NEFT, while the 
Training Institute will build expertise in cybersecurity, AI and other emerging technologies. 
 
4. In his welcome address, Reserve Bank Governor Shri Sanjay Malhotra expressed 
gratitude to the Hon’ble Prime Minister for his participation in the event. He emphasised 
the Reserve Bank’s commitment to leveraging emerging technologies, strengthening 
digital infrastructure, enhancing cybersecurity, developing indigenous technological 
capabilities and supporting the country’s aspiration to become a developed nation by 
2047. 
 
5. The event was attended by distinguished dignitaries from the Central Government, 
State Government, industry, academia, persons of eminence, Directors of the Central 
Board of the Reserve Bank, heads of banks, technology providers and senior officials of 
the Reserve Bank.

October 23, 2026 
RBI Bulletin – October 2026 
 
     Today, the Reserve Bank released the October 2026 issue of its monthly Bulletin. 
The Bulletin includes two speeches, four articles and current statistics. 
 
     The four articles are: I. State of the Economy; II. Transmission to Lending Rates of 
SCBs: Price versus Composition Effects in WALR; III. Performance of the NBFC 
Sector: Review for 2025; and IV. Nowcasting State-Level Economic Activity in India 
with Night-Time Light and Google Trends.  
 
I. State of the Economy 
 
     Renewed geopolitical frictions in West Asia and supply chain disruptions have 
amplified inflationary pressures, prompting major central banks to raise policy rates. 
Elevated sovereign bond yields in advanced economies (AEs) have also brought into 
focus concerns about fiscal sustainability and its implications for financial stability. The 
Indian economy continued to demonstrate strength as evidenced by high-frequency 
indicators across both industry and services. The headline Consumer Price Index 
(CPI) inflation edged up in September driven by a broad-based increase in food, fuel, 
and core components. Double-digit growth in merchandise exports during the first six 
months of 2026-27 helped in narrowing the trade deficit. FDI, ECB and remittance 
flows strengthened in August. Strong inflows under the FCNR(B) swap window 
augmented reserves. 
 
II. Transmission to Lending Rates of SCBs: Price versus Composition Effects 
in WALR  
 
By Yuvraj Kashyap, Kamal Gupta and Arvind Jha  
 
     This article analyses the transmission of monetary policy to the fresh lending rates 
of scheduled commercial banks by decomposing variations in the weighted average 
lending rate (WALR) into interest rate effects and compositional effects. Using an 
index-number based framework on bank and sector level lending rates and loan 
weights, the study examines the extent to which changes in the aggregate WALR 
reflect changes in lending rates and shifts in credit composition.

In response to a cumulative reduction of 125 basis points (bps) in the policy repo 
rate, the WALR on fresh lending declined by 93 bps, with interest rate effect of 80 
bps and composition effect of 13 bps during February 2025 to March 2026. 
• 
The movements in aggregate WALR reflect both repricing of loans and changes 
in the composition of credit across banks and sectors, highlighting the importance 
of both effects while assessing monetary policy transmission. 
 
III. Performance of the NBFC Sector: Review for 2025 
 
By Pallavi Pant, Monalisa Poali, Abhyuday Harsh, Brijesh P and Sona Chinngaihlian 
 
     This article assesses the performance of the non-banking financial company 
(NBFC) sector up to end-December 2025. It also provides a bird’s-eye-view of India’s 
financial system. Employing a text-mining approach, the article also explores the 
extent and nature of orientation towards artificial intelligence (AI) by select NBFCs. 
 
Highlights: 
 
• The NBFC sector continued to register double-digit y-o-y credit growth at end-
December 2025. 
• Share of bank borrowings showed a moderate rise indicating continued 
concentration in funding profile. Asset quality of the sector has continued to 
improve in recent years as reflected in consistent decline in NPA ratios.  
• Preliminary text-mining analysis shows that NBFCs are increasingly orienting 
towards AI for customer and financial applications, governance and digital 
infrastructure, and data analytics.

Google Trends 
  
By Bipul Ghosh, Narendra Singh and Sandhya Kuruganti  
 
     Timely measurement of state-level economic activity remains a challenge in India, 
as official Gross State Value Added (GSVA) data are released annually with a 
considerable lag. This study demonstrates how alternative data sources, specifically 
satellite-based night-time lights and digital search behaviour, can be used to generate 
high-frequency estimates of state-level economic activity. The framework is applied to 
three major states — Maharashtra, Karnataka and Gujarat. It shows how combining 
geospatial and behavioural signals can provide a real-time view of regional economic 
dynamics and strengthen short-term economic assessment. 
 
Highlights: 
 
• The combined use of night-time lights and Google Trends improves nowcast 
accuracy of quarterly GSVA growth relative to univariate approach. 
• The approach enables near real-time monitoring of state-level economies, 
improving early detection of turning points and shocks.

regulatory capital requirements, providing an indicative mapping of BI components, and 
incorporating additional clarifications.

October 21, 2026 
 
Minutes of the Monetary Policy Committee Meeting,  
October 5 to 7, 2026 
[Under Section 45ZL of the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934] 
 
     The sixty third meeting of the Monetary Policy Committee (MPC), constituted under 
Section 45ZB of the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934, was held during October 5 to 7, 
2026. 
 
2. 
The meeting was chaired by Shri Sanjay Malhotra, Governor and was attended 
by all the members – Dr. Nagesh Kumar, Director and Chief Executive, Institute for 
Studies in Industrial Development, New Delhi; Shri Saugata Bhattacharya, Economist, 
Mumbai; Professor Ram Singh, Director, Delhi School of Economics, Delhi; Dr. 
Poonam Gupta, Deputy Governor in charge of monetary policy and Shri Indranil 
Bhattacharyya, Executive Director (the officer of the Reserve Bank nominated by the 
Central Board under Section 45ZB(2)(c) of the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934). 
 
3. 
According to Section 45ZL of the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934, the Reserve 
Bank shall publish, on the fourteenth day after every meeting of the Monetary Policy 
Committee, the minutes of the proceedings of the meeting which shall include the 
following, namely: 
 
(a) the resolution adopted at the meeting of the Monetary Policy Committee;  
(b) the vote of each member of the Monetary Policy Committee, ascribed to such 
member, on the resolution adopted in the said meeting; and  
(c) the statement of each member of the Monetary Policy Committee under sub-
section (11) of section 45ZI on the resolution adopted in the said meeting. 
 
4. 
In the light of evolving developments on the global and domestic front, the MPC 
reviewed in detail the staff’s macroeconomic projections that included inputs from 
survey results and stakeholder consultations. The MPC also reviewed alternative 
scenarios around various risks to the outlook. Drawing on the above and after 
extensive discussions on the stance of monetary policy, the MPC adopted the 
resolution that is set out below.  
 
Resolution 
 
5. 
The Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) held its 63rd meeting from October 5 
to 7, 2026, under the chairmanship of Shri Sanjay Malhotra, Governor, Reserve Bank 
of India. The MPC members Dr. Nagesh Kumar, Shri Saugata Bhattacharya, Prof. 
Ram Singh, Dr. Poonam Gupta and Shri Indranil Bhattacharyya attended the meeting.

6. 
 After a detailed assessment of the evolving macroeconomic and financial 
developments and the outlook, the MPC voted unanimously to increase the policy repo 
rate under the liquidity adjustment facility (LAF) by 25 bps to 5.50 per cent. 
Consequently, the standing deposit facility (SDF) rate stands adjusted at 5.25 per cent 
and the marginal standing facility (MSF) rate and the Bank Rate at 5.75 per cent. The 
MPC also decided to change the stance to calibrated tightening.  
 
Growth and Inflation Outlook 
 
Global Outlook 
 
7. 
Since the last MPC meeting in August 2026, the re-escalation of the conflict in 
West Asia and the consequent sharp volatility in crude oil prices has kept the global 
economy in a state of flux. Global growth has remained resilient. Acceleration of 
inflation in key economies has prompted a shift towards hawkish monetary policy. The 
US Fed hiked by 25 bps in September. The Fed commentary thereafter along with rate 
tightening by major systemically important central banks have reinforced expectations 
of higher global policy rates. Tighter global financial market conditions coupled with 
fiscal sustainability concerns in major economies are keeping global bond yields at 
record high levels. With a resolution of the West Asia conflict remaining elusive, 
significant downside risks to the global outlook remain, including further tightening of 
global financial conditions, continuing elevated AI-related asset valuations and high 
public debt. 
 
Domestic Outlook 
 
8. 
Notwithstanding these persisting global headwinds, the Indian economy has 
remained resilient. As per National Statistics Office (NSO) estimates, real GDP growth 
in Q1:2026-27 at 7.8 per cent was higher than expected. Strong private consumption 
and fixed investment, rebound in merchandise exports and sustained buoyancy in 
services exports supported growth. On the supply side, the manufacturing sector grew 
at a robust pace. Services sector activity strengthened further, owing to buoyant 
domestic and external demand. 
  
9. 
In Q2, available high frequency indicators for July-August suggest sustained 
momentum in domestic economic activity. Domestic demand remains resilient and is 
well supported by robust external demand with merchandise exports registering 
double-digit growth.  
 
10. 
Looking ahead, global economic uncertainty will continue to have some bearing 
on domestic economic activity. While energy prices and supply chain pressures have 
continued, their near-term trajectory remains uncertain amidst the lingering West Asia 
conflict. Their adverse impact is being contained with active diversification of supply 
sources. Deficient south-west monsoon and strong El Niño conditions pose risks to 
agriculture sector’s outlook and rural demand, although healthy buffer of foodgrains 
and proactive policy interventions by the government are expected to mitigate the 
impact. Furthermore, continuing momentum in services and broadly stable 
employment conditions are likely to support urban demand. Strong capacity utilisation, 
robust credit flows and the government’s thrust on infrastructure are expected to 
sustain investment activity. While services exports are expected to remain buoyant, 
bilateral trade agreements should boost merchandise exports.  
   
3 
 
11. 
Taking all these factors into consideration, real GDP growth for 2026-27 is 
projected at 7.1 per cent, with Q2 at 7.2 per cent; Q3 at 6.9 per cent and Q4 at 6.8 per 
cent. Real GDP growth for Q1:2027-28 is projected at 7.1 per cent. The risks are 
evenly balanced (Chart 1). 
 
12. 
CPI inflation increased to 4.8 per cent in August 2026 from 4.5 per cent in July. 
While the increase has been predominantly on account of higher inflation in food and 
fuel groups, core inflation has also picked up indicating some signs of widening price 
pressures. Food price increases have become more broad based along with notable 
spikes in certain items such as sugar and onion. The uptick in fuel inflation in August 
largely reflected unfavourable base effects. Core inflation increased to 4.2 per cent 
and core inflation, excluding precious metals, increased to 2.9 per cent in August. The 
weighted share of items in headline CPI recording inflation above 4 per cent increased 
steadily to about 37 per cent in August.  
 
13. 
The near-term outlook on inflation points towards continued pressures from 
supply side on account of the deficient monsoon, ongoing El Niño conditions and high 
energy and other commodity prices, the pass through of which is still continuing. 
Considering all factors, CPI inflation is projected to be 5.2 per cent for 2026-27 with 
Q2 at 4.9 per cent; Q3 at 6.0 per cent; and Q4 at 5.7 per cent (Chart 2). Inflation for 
Q1:2027-28 is projected at 5.6 per cent with risks being evenly balanced. Core inflation 
is projected at 4.4 per cent for 2026-27. 
  
 
 
 
Rationale for Monetary Policy Decisions 
 
14. 
The MPC noted that the global context on account of geopolitical developments 
remains challenging. Nonetheless, the Indian economy has been strong. The 
economic momentum remains broad-based. The economy is expected to remain 
resilient.  
 
15. 
In the light of available data, it is clear that inflation and its outlook are not 
benign as they were last year with headline CPI inflation expected to average almost 
5.8 per cent in the next three quarters and core inflation projected at 4.4 per cent this 
year. In this milieu, recalibrating the policy rate is imperative. 
4 
 
 
16. 
As regards supply side inflation, monetary policy primarily acts by curtailing 
second round effects (inflation expectations and firm level pricing behaviour, etc.), 
which take time to manifest and are difficult to extract from available data. Apart from 
data related to inflation expectations and firm level pricing behaviour, indicators of 
generalisation of inflation like core inflation and diffusion indices are used for this 
purpose. It may, however, be kept in mind that it is difficult to distinguish between the 
second-round effects and the indirect impact of supply side pressures (in production 
cost through energy and other inputs) as both are present in these indicators.  While 
there is some evidence of elevated inflation expectations and generalisation of 
inflation, there are only limited signs of supply side pressures getting embedded in 
pricing behaviour. 
  
17. 
Similarly, while there is limited evidence of demand side pressures, risks in view 
of strong growth in monetary and credit aggregates exist. 
 
18. 
Considering all these factors, the MPC unanimously voted to increase the policy 
repo rate by 25 basis points to 5.50 per cent.  The MPC also decided to change the 
stance to calibrated tightening. It only signals that given the current conditions, rate 
cuts are off the table in the near term and policy action ahead can only be a rate hike 
or a pause, depending on the evolving conditions and the outlook. The duration and 
extent of rate hike cycle would be contingent on the actual growth-inflation 
developments and outlook, especially that of underlying inflation, the extent of 
broadening of price pressures and second round effects of the supply shock, as also 
the impact of demand impulses. 
  
19. 
Two members - Dr. Nagesh Kumar and Prof. Ram Singh - were of the view that 
the stance be retained at neutral. 
 
20. 
The MPC remains committed to its price stability mandate and will endeavour 
to progressively align inflation with its target.  
 
21. 
The minutes of the MPC’s meeting will be published on October 21, 2026. 
 
22. 
The next meeting of the MPC is scheduled for December 2 to 4, 2026.

Statement by Dr. Nagesh Kumar 
 
23. 
The 7.8% GDP growth logged by the Indian economy in Q1:FY2027, coming 
as it does against the backdrop of the West Asia conflict and continued trade policy 
uncertainties, is impressive, highlighting its resilience. The Q1 growth was 
5 
 
underpinned by robust manufacturing growth of 9.2%, which is encouraging because 
of its direct and indirect job-creating effects. There are indications that the growth 
momentum is being carried through into Q2, as borne out by a healthy rate of 
gross fixed capital formation (GFCF), which was 34.3% in Q1:FY27 compared to 
31.4% in Q1:FY26. If this 290-basis-point jump sustains, it would be very good for the 
economy, paving the way for the private investment cycle to gain momentum and drive 
industrial growth. The expansion of industrial credit also supports the view that the 
private investment cycle may finally be taking off. Similarly, the capital goods sector 
has been posting double-digit growth for the past 4 months, which is consistent with 
the robust GFCF and credit growth. A number of big investment proposals for data 
centres are coming up from big IT majors/global tech companies, and GCCs are 
augmenting their presence in the country. Hence, the projected growth for FY2026-27 
has been raised to 7.1% from 6.7% at the time of the previous policy. 
 
24. 
Merchandise exports have also shown robust growth in spite of global trade 
policy uncertainties, along with those of services exports, helping to keep the current 
account deficit in a manageable range of around 1% of GDP. The FCNR(B) scheme 
of RBI has helped to bring substantial inflows of NRI deposits which, besides helping 
to stabilise the exchange rate of the rupee, will lead to a significant balance of 
payments surplus in 2026-27. Going forward, the India-EU FTA, among others, which 
is likely to come into force towards the beginning of 2027, is likely to boost India’s 
exports, especially of labour-intensive goods, by giving Indian products a level playing 
field vis-à-vis peers such as Vietnam and Bangladesh, for the first time. 
 
25. 
The inflationary outlook, on the other hand, remains challenging due to a 
combination of factors, including the deficient monsoon, rising crude oil prices, 
precious metals prices remaining at elevated levels, and exchange rate depreciation, 
leading to a revision of the forecast for headline inflation for 2026-27 by 20 basis points 
from 5.0% at the last policy to 5.2% and core inflation by 10 basis points to 4.4%. 
While inflation is driven largely by supply-side factors and does not show any signs of 
overheating of the economy nor of generalisation, it is important to manage inflationary 
expectations.  
  
26. 
Keeping in mind the need to manage the inflationary outlook, I vote for a 25-
basis-point increase in the repo rate.  In view of the continued geopolitical and trade 
policy uncertainties, I feel that a neutral stance remains appropriate.  
 
Statement by Shri Saugata Bhattacharya 
 
27. 
Since the August ‘26 review, global financial conditions have tightened 
significantly. Energy prices have again risen. El Niño led weather disruptions have 
resulted in an increase in prices of many agricultural commodities, particularly of edible 
oils, sugar and, to an extent, cereals. 
     
28. 
Most major central banks, responding to global macro-financial conditions, 
have adjusted their policy rates upwards. Benchmark yields have risen sharply across 
multiple G20 countries, and research reports suggest this is partly a result of rising 
term premia now sought by investors.1  
 
 
1 BIS Quarterly Review Sep ’26, “Yields Climb, yet Risk Appetite stays firm”.  
6 
 
29. 
In India, since the August 2026 review, some of the upside risks to inflation 
have started materialising. Data increasingly suggests that price pressures are getting 
entrenched into the economic system. Input prices, recorded in Wholesale Price 
Indices, have been printing close to 9% yoy. Media reports and enterprise surveys 
suggest that these input costs are being passed on to consumer prices. While 
‘underlying inflation’ has thus far remained more subdued, and might implicitly be a 
signal of some residual demand weakness, trends in CPI inflation components indicate 
that a presumed slack relative to the potential output – if a slack at all even exists at 
present – appears to be closing. 
  
30. 
MPC growth forecasts and official estimates reinforce current data, market 
reports, media news and forward-looking surveys suggesting that economic activity is 
– and will remain – resilient. High bank credit growth, earlier mostly restricted to the 
retail segment and to an extent MSMEs, have now dispersed into virtually all sectors 
and segments. 
  
31. 
India’s external balance, however, remains a concern. The balance of 
payments shows some vulnerabilities, particularly given the tight global financial 
environment. At the very least, maintaining a certain gap between India and G7 
interest rates is important for attracting debt capital flows. At the same time, too rapid 
a policy rate adjustment risks constricting growth and hence growth-led capital flows.  
 
32. 
In this context, might the broad monetary policy environment in India now be 
too accommodative?  Inflation risks and financial markets suggest it is. Growth is 
resilient enough to permit a closer focus on an incipient inflation persistence. The 
current and forecast level of real interest rates do not seem consistent with levels 
required for ensuring price stability. The real natural rate of interest (pertaining to Q4 
of FY23-24) estimated this to be 1.4-1.9%. It is very likely that the slack of current 
output from potential will have shrunk, compared to the immediate post-COVID period.  
 
33. 
Hence, the totality of information indicates a strong economic case at this time 
for tightening monetary policy, to bring inflation closer to the target sooner rather than 
later and anchor inflation expectations.  
 
34. 
Domestic financial conditions have tightened significantly. This, to an extent, 
mitigates the need for large domestic monetary policy actions. Hence, the magnitude 
and pace of monetary policy adjustment needs to be carefully calibrated to balance 
the multiple trade-offs from these actions – inflation vs growth, credit vs deposits, 
domestic vs external and more.  A data dependent approach is best to deal with the 
broad range of possible outcomes in this uncertain economic environment. 
  
35. 
Hence, I vote to increase the policy repo rate by 25 basis points. Given the 
upside risks to inflation, it is also appropriate to change the stance to calibrated 
tightening. 
 
Statement by Prof. Ram Singh 
 
36. 
Since the last MPC meeting, inflationary pressures have hardened in most 
leading economies, prompting their monetary authorities to adopt a hawkish 
stance.  Domestic inflation and its near-term trajectory have also turned less benign. 
Evidence suggests inflation has generalised beyond the direct effects of fuel, energy, 
and commodity prices since the onset of the West Asia conflict. Emerging evidence 
7 
 
points to indirect effects (firms passing these cost increases onto the prices of the 
goods and services they provide). Diffusion indices and the core inflation trajectory 
provide some evidence. The number of items in the CPI basket rising above 4% has 
increased. The core is projected at 4.4 per cent this financial year. Non-food, non-fuel 
core inflation also climbed to 4.2% in August 2026, at least in part because producers 
raised their selling prices. Furthermore, the RBI’s September household survey 
showed the 3-month median inflation expectation jumped to 9.9%, reflecting 
households' anticipation of a higher cost of living. 
   
37. 
These effects and their impact on headline CPI have been moderate so 
far.  However, combined with possible demand-side pressures, driven by strong credit 
growth, the economy faces the risk of supply-side pressures becoming more 
widespread in the coming months.  Headline CPI inflation is expected to remain 
elevated, averaging almost 5.8 per cent over the next three quarters, nudging the 
upper limit of the FIT tolerance band. Additionally, at the current repo rate level, the 
projected inflation trajectory will render the real rate negative, generating perverse 
saving-consumption trade-offs. 
 
38. 
To realign the inflation trajectory towards the target, and from the real repo rate 
perspective, a calibrated increase in the repo rate is needed. The duration and 
magnitude of the rate hike required to meet these objectives would depend on the 
emerging growth-inflation outlook. The MPC will have to remain vigilant about the pace 
of inflation generalisation to respond in a timely and effective way. For now, there is a 
case for incremental, mild repo rate hikes, not high-for-long rates. 
 
39. 
I do not favour shifting the stance from neutral to tightening mode, as it may 
signal an extended cycle of rate hikes. This, in turn, can neutralise the benefits of 
growth-supportive monetary and fiscal policies in the recent past. Current inflation is 
primarily due to supply-side factors, rising fuel, food, and commodity prices, and their 
effects. The classic signs of economic overheating —such as a wage-price spiral or 
demand-driven capacity overstretch or abnormal growth in private consumption and 
capex —are largely absent. The Q1 growth rate (7.8%) is in line with the average 
growth rate in recent years (7.9% during FY 2021-22 to 2025-26). Growth is expected 
to moderate in the coming quarters, especially in sectors like real estate and 
automobiles, as the GST boost peters out. PMI manufacturing and services both show 
some signs of moderation.  
 
40. 
Expectations of significant rate increases can undermine demand not only in 
interest rate-sensitive sectors such as vehicles, real estate, and discretionary 
spending, but also drag on recent momentum in private investment. Coming on the 
heels of stress on the farm sector due to below-normal rains and El Niño, rising input 
costs and global uncertainty, significant rate hikes would hurt profit margins and the 
sustainability of capex plans of large and small firms. 
 
41. 
Therefore, I vote for a 25-bps increase in the repo rate to 5.50% without 
changing the stance. 
 
Statement by Shri Indranil Bhattacharyya 
 
42. 
Notwithstanding an adverse external backdrop and despite an erratic domestic 
monsoon, the Indian economy has fared much better than expectations with economic 
8 
 
activity on a sound footing and poised to register more than 7 per cent growth in 2026-
27.  
 
43. 
On the inflation front, there are, however, reasons for concern. Inflation is 
clearly on the rise, averaging about 5.8 per cent in the immediate three quarters, driven 
by food and fuel prices. The weighted share of items in the CPI basket experiencing 
inflation above 6 per cent has increased noticeably in August, as suggested by the 
diffusion index. Core inflation (CPI excluding food and fuel) also indicates a similar 
shift in distribution, albeit of a lower magnitude.  The momentum of underlying inflation 
is also high as evident from the weighted median and trimmed mean measures in 
recent months.2 These are corroborated by the latest round of survey findings which 
suggests that inflation expectations are significantly higher in both the urban and rural 
areas.3 Moreover, there is increasing evidence of pass-through of input cost pressures 
in certain segments such as restaurants and cooked meals. PMI surveys and producer 
price indices also suggest some pent-up pass-through. Greater pass-through is 
expected going ahead, especially when demand conditions are strong. 
  
44. 
Therefore, the inflation outlook merits greater attention, given supply side 
pressures from crude and food prices are unlikely to relent quickly. With demand 
holding strong and in the wake of strong growth in monetary and credit aggregates, 
the interplay of both supply and demand factors could ratchet up inflation pressures 
significantly in the period ahead. Therefore, I feel it is better to set aside the 
“cautiousness bias”4 and act in a pre-emptive manner at this juncture rather than wait 
and watch.  Accordingly, I vote for a 25-bps policy rate hike. Going ahead, the 
trajectory of the policy path would be calibrated based on the evolving macroeconomic 
developments and emerging inflation prints. Given the present global and domestic 
circumstances, rate cuts are not an option in the near term. Therefore, I feel it is also 
appropriate to change the stance from neutral to calibrated tightening. While the 
neutral stance is consistent with all three policy options (cut, hike and pause), 
calibrated tightening conveys an unequivocally clear message that rate hikes or pause 
are the only options in the near term, depending on the evolving outlook. Besides 
signalling, this would also reaffirm our commitment to price stability as the primary 
objective of monetary policy. 
 
Statement by Dr. Poonam Gupta 
  
45. 
The global backdrop has continued to evolve since the last policy meeting, 
feeding heightened uncertainty. Two developments in particular stand out: first, the 
flare-up in the West Asia conflict and persistently elevated oil prices; second, the 
implications of high demand for financial resources from sovereigns and the private 
sector in some advanced economies on global interest rates and cost of funding in 
other countries including emerging market economies.  
 
2 Various measures of trimmed mean (5%, 10% and 25%) suggest that it has increased from the range 2.2-2.7 per cent in March 
to 3.7-4.2 per cent in August 2026. Similarly, the weighted median has increased from 2 per cent to 3.5 per cent over the same 
period. 
3 In the Reserve Bank’s September 2026 survey, urban households’ inflation expectations for the next three months as well as 
one year ahead rose by 70 bps and 60 bps, respectively. According to the bi-monthly Rural Consumer Confidence Survey 
(RCCS), the current perception of inflation in rural and semiurban households increased by 70 bps while it rose by 50 bps for 
expectations one-year ahead in September 2026. 
4 From monetary policy perspective, concerns about uncertainty create a cautiousness bias: acting less is justified when the 
private sector’s expectations of inflation are assumed to remain unchanged, but acting less may lead to sharp spike in inflation 
and unhinge inflation expectations. In response to the de-anchoring of expectations, the central bank can easily end up tightening 
much more than it initially intended to do, hurting growth but without succeeding in aligning inflation back to its target quickly (see 
Stephane Dupraz, Sophie Guilloux-Nefussi and Adrian Penalver (2023), A Pitfall of Cautiousness in Monetary Policy, International 
Journal of Central Banking, Vol 19(3), August. 
9 
 
 
46. 
Domestically, the economy has done exceptionally well, growing at 7.8 per cent 
in Q1:2026-27, well above the forecast in the August policy. A range of high-frequency 
indicators support the growth momentum in Q2 as well. Meanwhile, inflation, primarily 
driven by food, fuel and gold, with limited generalisation to core, has inched up to 4.5 
per cent in July and further to 4.8 per cent in August. Consequently, the MPC has 
revised upward its inflation forecast to 5.2 per cent while increasing real GDP growth 
forecast for 2026-27 to 7.1 per cent. Inflation is projected to accelerate to 6.0 per cent 
in Q3 before moderating to 5.7 per cent in Q4 and 5.6 per cent in Q1 next year. 
  
47. 
At this point in time, inflation is mostly driven by external supply-side shocks, 
with insignificant signs of it becoming entrenched or impacting inflation expectations. 
Yet, with projections indicating the likelihood of headline inflation hitting the upper 
tolerance limit of 6 per cent, one may not want to wait for more definitive evidence of 
generalisation, and instead be mindful of the fact that monetary policy works with a 
lag. 
 
48. 
In fact, in the post pandemic inflation targeting period, whenever inflation has 
reached or breached the lower or upper tolerance limits, appropriate policy action has 
been taken. This has helped retain the credibility of the framework and has kept 
inflation expectations aligned to the target. Thus, rather than waiting any longer, in 
view of rising inflation and resilient growth, I favour raising the policy repo rate by 25 
bps in this policy.  
 
49. 
Meanwhile, inflationary pressures are mounting around the world, driven by 
high fuel and commodity prices. Domestically, weather-related adversities and global 
oil and commodity prices may continue to put upward pressure on headline inflation. 
At some point, a larger pass-through of input costs to output prices may materialise. 
Under these circumstances, it is conceivable that a further increase in the policy rate 
might be needed to keep inflation low and inflationary expectations anchored. The 
pace, extent, and duration of such actions would depend on the incoming data on 
inflation, its diffusion, and evidence of second-round effects. 
  
50. 
Hence, I propose to change the stance to calibrated tightening, which would be 
consistent with any such warranted future course of action. 
 
Statement by Shri Sanjay Malhotra 
 
51. 
Amidst the turbulent global backdrop, the Indian economy has shown 
remarkable resilience. Growth for the full year 2026-27 is now projected at 7.1 per 
cent, 40 bps higher than the projection of 6.7 per cent in August. 
 
52. 
Inflationary pressures are, however, building up. Headline CPI is projected to 
touch the upper tolerance band in Q3 and remain significantly above 5 per cent in the 
next two quarters. 
 
53. 
In terms of the diffusion index, there are increasing signs of generalisation of 
inflation as 37 per cent of the commodities in the CPI basket had inflation above 4 per 
cent in August – it was merely 20 per cent in March. While core inflation increased 
from 3.9 per cent in July to 4.2 per cent in August, core inflation, excluding precious 
metals, increased to 2.9 per cent in August, driven by a strong momentum of 0.5 per 
cent. Underlying inflation, as measured by core ex precious metals is also anticipated 
10 
 
to move above target in the coming months.  This indicates a normalisation of inflation 
from the benign levels seen earlier. 
  
54. 
As regards supply side inflation requiring a monetary policy response, it is 
pertinent to mention that monetary policy primarily acts by curtailing second round 
effects (wage expectations and firm level pricing behaviour) of a supply shock. It is 
difficult to distinguish between the second-round effects and the indirect impact of 
supply side pressures (in production cost through energy and other inputs) as both are 
present in core inflation. 
 
55. 
Similarly, there are risks of demand side pressures in view of the growth in 
monetary and credit aggregates. 
 
56. 
Considering the above growth-inflation dynamics, I consider it appropriate to 
recalibrate the policy rate. Accordingly, I vote for a 25-bps hike in the policy rate. The 
duration and extent of the rate hiking cycle would be contingent on the actual growth-
inflation developments and outlook, especially that of underlying inflation, the 
broadening of price pressures, second round effects of the supply shock, and the 
impact of demand impulses. Nevertheless, I feel it is appropriate to change the stance 
to calibrated tightening, essentially signalling that rate cuts are off the table in the near 
term and policy action ahead can only be a rate hike or a pause, depending on the 
evolving circumstances and the outlook.
